Procurement Lead at Supabase

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (771 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realworkfromanywhere

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that we’re looking for a Procurement Lead to own the commercial and vendor-management function for Supabase.
  • This is a lead role for the Procurement function.
  • Own vendor relationships: run our primary cloud and SaaS vendor relationships end-to-end (AWS, GCP, Cloudflare, CloudQuery, ClickHouse, and more), leading renewals and negotiations alongside Finance and Legal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that we’re looking for a Procurement Lead to own the commercial and vendor-management function for Supabase. You’ll run our cloud and SaaS vendor relationships end-to-end (AWS, GCP, Cloudflare, CloudQuery, ClickHouse, and more), leading negotiations and renewals, enforcing procurement governance, and applying our VIA operating model (Visibility, Insights, Actions) to keep vendor spend disciplined and well-governed. You’ll work closely with Finance, Engineering, Legal, and our vendor partners.

This is a lead role for the Procurement function. The operating model, the source of truth for vendor spend, and the standards are yours to define, against a clear position: this is a FinOps role first, not a pure procurement desk. You'll own the technical and analytical side of vendor management, reporting, efficiency, and the commercial interface across the manufacturer, while keeping procurement governance tight. It's ideal for someone fluent across finance and engineering, who thrives in async, fast-moving environments, and wants to build a function from the ground up rather than inherit one.

Own vendor relationships: run our primary cloud and SaaS vendor relationships end-to-end (AWS, GCP, Cloudflare, CloudQuery, ClickHouse, and more), leading renewals and negotiations alongside Finance and Legal.

Run procurement governance: enforce our competitive-bid process for incoming requests and manage larger procurement through our managed-procurement partner, keeping oversight and accountability with FinOps.

Industry observers note that people management: Build a healthy, high-trust team culture in a remote-first, globally distributed environment. Run 1:1s, performance management, career development, and onboarding for your direct report(s).Handle people admin (leave, time off, etc.) for your team.

According to recent reports, manage team’s delivery and accountability: Own the team's roadmap and project management (Linear), driving accountability and clear milestones. Manage workflow intake and Slack triage. Own the team's weekly updates and keep stakeholders aligned without creating overhead.

Drive commercial VIA: own spend visibility and unit economics, surface licensing and usage inefficiency before it becomes a surprise, and drive renewals, right-sizing, and tooling consolidation to realized savings.

Recent findings suggest that build reporting and governance: vendor and SaaS cost reporting is the unowned gap today and your highest-leverage area in the first year. Build the dashboards and reporting hands-on, partner with our data teams to scale them, and own the governance layer (spend policies, thresholds, accountability).

Coordinate the cloud efficiency program: keep optimization initiatives visible and tracked from commitment to realized savings, partnering with Engineering without taking over their delivery.

Have 8+ years in vendor/commercial management, procurement, FinOps, or technical/financial analysis, at a senior, function-owning level.

Have owned vendor relationships, contract negotiations, and renewals, and treat them as a lever on unit economics.

Have run procurement governance such as competitive-bid processes, benchmark analysis, approval thresholds, or managed-procurement partners.

Have high judgment and can hold a position and drive alignment without positional authority.

Build cost dashboards and reporting hands-on (SQL, BI tools), and are comfortable with vendor and cloud spend data (AWS, GCP, SaaS billing) and licensing/usage analysis.

Communicate clearly across both technical and non-technical audiences.

Have experience in async or globally distributed teams.

Are energized by building a function from the ground up and navigating ambiguity.

Industry observers note that we hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

It has been revealed that every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the tech giant. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

According to recent reports, supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are crucial to us.

Industry observers note that once a year, the entire manufacturer gathers in a newly introduced city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

In a recent development, we operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

Supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F).

We move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

Legal Assistant at Atticus

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (811 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realworkfromanywhere

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, at any given time, 16 million Americans are experiencing a crisis that requires urgent help from our legal system or government.
  • Sources indicate that atticus makes it easy for any sick or injured American to get life-changing aid.
  • So far, we’ve helped hundreds of thousands of people access over $10 billion in life-changing aid —and earned over 20,000 five-star reviews.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, at any given time, 16 million Americans are experiencing a crisis that requires urgent help from our legal system or government. The right assistance could transform their lives. But today, most never get it.

Sources indicate that atticus makes it easy for any sick or injured American to get life-changing aid. Our mission is to tear down barriers between people in crisis and the aid they deserve. In the last six years, we’ve become the leading platform connecting people with disabilities to government benefits. We also help victims of accidents, misconduct, and violence get compensation from insurance.

So far, we’ve helped hundreds of thousands of people access over $10 billion in life-changing aid —and earned over 20,000 five-star reviews. And we’re just getting started.

We've raised more than $100 million from top VC firms like Forerunner, Google Ventures, and True Ventures, and we’re on our way to creating a category defining business assisting Americans in need.

Each day, thousands of people seek our help getting disability benefits or insurance compensation. They’re intimidated by the process, unsure where to turn, and desperate for good advice.

According to recent reports, as a Legal Assistant at Atticus, your job is to ensure they get and stay on the right path. This job is different from that of a traditional legal assistant. The job mixes responsibilities in any good legal assistant’s comfort zone (build client relationships; support paralegals and attorneys in filing and managing claims) with those unique to being an operator in a fast-growing tech firm (help Marketing source clients who’d be great in testimonials, or user test fresh tools for Product).

In a typical week you might do any of the following:.

Make contact with a client that’s in danger of slipping through the cracks at SSA, and help get their case back on track.

Work with a client’s team to run down missing paperwork at SSA.

Take on an inefficient workflow that’s slowing the team down (e.g., processing case updates), scope an improvement, get team buy-in, and execute the improvement.

It has been revealed that this role is a rare opportunity to join a fast-growing Series C startup and do meaningful social impact work. It’s designed to be a path to building expertise in the fields of law you support and taking on greater responsibilities over time (e.g. becoming a paralegal).

You have a Bachelor’s degree from a four-year university with strong academic performance.

You have experience in a professional role that required a substantial amount of customer-facing work and/or administrative tasks.

You are a resourceful team-player ready to dive into a scrappy startup environment where you will learn promptly and get your hands dirty.

You are comfortable in a variety of interpersonal conversations; you can be empathetic and kind when speaking with people in a moment of crisis, and can be thoughtful and organized when interacting with attorneys or the SSA.

You have a demonstrated commitment to doing good and helping people.

You have professional experience helping others apply for government benefits.

You have experience at a startup or other fast-paced, agile environment.

Industry observers note that we are strongly committed to building a diverse team. If you’re from a background that’s underrepresented in tech, we’d love to meet you.

This is a rare opportunity to join a startup that has strong traction (substantial funding, well-respected backers, tremendous growth, and many happy customers) but is still small enough that you can have a huge impact and play a role in shaping our culture.

We’re a certified B Corporation tackling a critical social problem. Our mission to help people in need drives everything we do, and your work here will touch many lives.

We offer competitive pay — including equity for every employee — and generous benefits:.

Medical and dental insurance with 100% of employees and their families premiums covered.

15 vacation days & ~20 paid holidays each year (including two weeks at the end-of-year).

$1,000/year reimbursable stipend for education and training outside of work.

Up to $1,200/year student loan repayment assistance.

401(k) match and optional HSA/FSA.

Humble, thoughtful, smart, fun colleagues.

According to recent reports, we anticipate the base salary band for this role will be between $50,000 and $75,000 in addition to equity and benefits. The salary at offer will be determined by a number of factors such as candidate’s experience, knowledge, skills and abilities, as well as internal equity among our team.

This job is fully remote and we’re committed to empowering everyone with flexibility. Work remotely, and travel to LA (on the organization dime) as needed to be with your colleagues – usually quarterly, plus offsites. We care a lot about building a great culture and we think some interactions need to happen in person, so we put a lot of thought into retreats, offsites, and other ways to gather.

Public Policy Lead - US at Kindred

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, kindred is a members-only home swapping platform that unlocks the ability to live a travel-rich lifestyle through the power of community.
  • Kindred is revolutionizing the “third option” of travel accommodation, compared to short-term rentals and hotels.
  • To support that momentum, Kindred has raised over $150M in capital from some of the most credible investors in Silicon Valley, including Index Ventures, Andreessen Horowitz, Upcoming Enterprise Associates, Bessemer Venture Partners, Caffeinated Capital, Elad Gil, and founders of companies like Opendoor, Figma, ClassPass, and more.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, kindred is a members-only home swapping platform that unlocks the ability to live a travel-rich lifestyle through the power of community. By exchanging primary residences with trusted peers, renters and owners alike can match with Kindred spirits and explore latest destinations without breaking the bank.

Kindred is revolutionizing the “third option” of travel accommodation, compared to short-term rentals and hotels. Since launching in 2022, Kindred has grown to a global community of 300,000 members across 150+ cities and puts home swapping on the map as a radically more affordable, responsible, and connected way to travel.

To support that momentum, Kindred has raised over $150M in capital from some of the most credible investors in Silicon Valley, including Index Ventures, Andreessen Horowitz, Upcoming Enterprise Associates, Bessemer Venture Partners, Caffeinated Capital, Elad Gil, and founders of companies like Opendoor, Figma, ClassPass, and more.

Kindred’s co-founders are proven leaders from the early team at Opendoor ($15B+ exit), who have each built and scaled products that today generate $1B+ annual revenue combined.

We’re looking for the world’s top builders, executors, and believers to help us make travel more meaningful.

You can learn more about us in Forbes and The Latest York Times.

This is Kindred’s first dedicated public policy hire. You’ll join a three-person legal and policy team (reporting to the General Counsel) and own the execution of Kindred’s public policy and government relations efforts, with a focus on North American markets but covering additional markets as necessary.

The role is primarily focused on proactive advocacy to shape the policy environment for home-swapping. You’ll build relationships with elected officials, regulators, and industry groups. You’ll commission and manage economic impact research. You’ll develop city-level partnerships that normalize home-swapping as a category distinct from other travel categories. You’ll also develop working familiarity with the tax, housing, and accommodation regulations that intersect with Kindred’s model, and help parse how those frameworks apply (or don’t) to credit-based home-swapping. You’ll do all of this initially as a team of one, with outside consultants to support you and a path to building a team as the company grows and the function matures.

Execute Kindred’s public policy strategy with an emphasis on proactive advocacy.

Sources indicate that build and maintain relationships with elected officials, regulators, and staff at the local, state/provincial, and national levels. Represent Kindred in meetings, hearings, coalition convenings, and industry events.

Recent findings suggest that track proposed housing, short-term rental, tax, and platform regulations that could impact Kindred’s model, identifying where Kindred’s credit-based, non-commercial structure creates meaningful regulatory distinctions. Use AI-assisted tools and other technology to monitor developments across jurisdictions.

Further develop and evolve Kindred’s core policy narrative and positioning materials. Draft position papers, comment letters, testimony, and advocacy materials.

Propose and negotiate city-level partnerships that promote and normalize home-swapping. Build relationships with housing advocacy organizations, tourism boards, trade associations, and aligned industry coalitions.

Commission and manage third-party economic analyses on the impact of Kindred’s model, collaborating with internal business teams and outside consulting firms.

Identify, evaluate, and manage outside consultants cost-effectively (lobbyists, policy advisors, research firms).

Partner with internal teams to develop externally facing materials and data packages for stakeholder engagements.

Coordinate with the General Counsel on lobbying compliance, political activity disclosures, and regulatory filings.

7–10 years of experience in public policy, with at least 3 years at a technology manufacturer or similar fast paced environment.

Experience building or meaningfully contributing to building a public policy or government relations function, not just operating within an established one.

Track record of productive relationships with elected officials, regulators, and policy stakeholders.

Experience managing outside consultants, lobbyists, or policy advisors across multiple jurisdictions.

Strong written and verbal communication skills, including experience drafting policy position papers, advocacy materials, or regulatory comments.

Experience with policy matters at the city and state level in the United States, with an interest in policy work in upcoming jurisdictions.

Fluency with AI tools and a willingness to integrate them into policy monitoring, research, and content development workflows.

Willingness to operate as an individual contributor while building the function, with the judgment to know when to engage outside support.

Experience in or adjacent to the sharing economy, home-sharing, travel, housing, or short-term rental sectors.

Experience at a growth-stage company (under 500 employees).

Familiarity with vacation/short-term rental, housing, and land use regulations, as well as related tax regulations.

Comfort with detailed regulatory analysis: ability to read and interpret statutes, ordinances, and administrative rules, and translate their implications into actionable policy positions. A law degree and legal practice experience is a plus but not required.

Build something new: You’ll help define the function and shape how Kindred engages with governments and regulators from the ground up.

Path to leadership: As the manufacturer and function grow, this role offers the opportunity to greater leadership.

Our openings may span more than one career level. The base salary offered depends on factors such as experience, transferable skills, business needs, impact, and market data.

Competitive cash compensation and equity.

Flexible time off, plus 12 paid holidays per year.

21 credits per year to stay in Kindred homes.

$4,000 annual travel stipend to help offset travel-related costs.

Remote-first and remote-flexible work environment, with opportunities to work from anywhere and gather in person, including at Kindred HQ in San Francisco.

Regular team and organization offsites to connect, collaborate, and build together.

A vibrant, inclusive, and highly skilled team that ferociously protects team chemistry.

A culture of high standards, feedback, and continual growth.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, kit is the email marketing platform experts choose to grow their audience, deepen their relationships, and build a business around the work they love. For coaches, YouTubers, authors, podcasters, and other creatives, there isn't a better marketing hub to rely on to grow audiences, automate email marketing, and sell digital products — all within one platform.More importantly, there isn't a team more committed to helping creators earn a living. We're on a mission to help creators earn $1 billion using our creator marketing platform. We have always been 100% independent and 100% remote.We are proud to have built a product that our customers love, and we look for people who have enthusiasm and belief in our mission, vision, and values to join our team. We're also embracing AI thoughtfully — both in how we build and how we hire to ensure our team is adaptable, innovative, and ready for what's next.

    Kit's most established creators run real companies, with teams, large lists, dedicated sending needs, and a buying process that our self-serve motion wasn't built to serve. Because this part of our business is growing, we're looking for a Senior Product Marketing Manager, Scaling Creators to own how Kit wins, lands, and expands these businesses through a sales-assisted motion that sits alongside our self-serve product.

    It has been revealed that you'll define who this buyer is, write the story that resonates and wins with them, and build the GTM strategy to drive inbound pipeline for our sales team. When these creators choose Kit and grow on it, they build more valuable businesses, and that's the outcome this role exists for.

    This is a full-time individual contributor role ideal for someone who has added an upmarket sales-led motion to a product-led firm before and wants their work measured in win rate and deal size.

    According to recent reports, you'll report to Christina Lhi, Head of Marketing, and work alongside two other experienced Product Marketing Managers on Kit's product marketing team. Together, you'll keep the self-serve and sales-assisted stories feeling like one Kit.

    You'll spend a lot of your time with:.

    Our sales leadership, on who we sell to, the deal toolkit, enablement, and win/loss.

    Account Executives and Solutions Consultants, on demo narratives, discovery, and technical and migration proof.

    Product, on packaging, releases, and roadmap input.

    RevOps and analytics, on how accounts get routed to sales, attribution, and pricing decisions.

    Creator Success, on case studies, customer references, and expansion plays.

    Demand gen, content, and events, on campaigns and events for established creators.

    First Week: Dive into our onboarding curriculum in Notion and learn Kit's product, pricing, and current positioning. Attend Get-To-Know-You (GTKY) meetings with marketing, sales, Solutions Consultants, RevOps, and Creator Success. Get access to our CRM, call recordings, and product analytics, and start listening to recent sales calls. Understand how product marketing currently works at Kit.

    In a recent development, first Month: Shadow 15+ sales calls and talk with 10 established creators, including recent wins, losses, and churned accounts. Audit the sales content reps use today and how product usage at the moment routes accounts to sales. Set baselines with RevOps for win rate, sales cycle, deal size, and expansion revenue. Share a written point of view with the entire growth team on who our established creator buyer is and the three biggest gaps in how we sell to them. And an action plan on how we can win these creators.

    In a recent development, first Year: Sales runs on messaging and tools you built, pitch with confidence and we drive 2X inbound MQLs from when you started. You’ll own and lead our channel strategy, setting the vision, driving cross-functional alignment, and partnering with Marketing to bring it to life. You'll run a quarterly win/loss program and share what you learn openly, build a clear path for sales leads on our website, and make sure introduces that matter to larger accounts ship with both a self-serve and a sales-assisted version. Your work has a direct impact on helping Kit reach $100,000,000 ARR while protecting the self-serve engine that got us here.

    Segmentation and buyer definition: turning firmographic and product usage data into a clear picture of who to sell to and when.

    Messaging and positioning for a sales-assisted buyer, including competitive differentiation and objection handling.

    Sales enablement that reps actually use: demo narratives, discovery guides, business cases, and battlecards.

    Writing and storytelling that turns product depth into a business case a non-technical buyer can act on.

    Working with CRM, product analytics, and pipeline data to measure funnel conversion, win rate, and deal size.

    Customer and market/competitor research, including win/loss interviews and call analysis.

    Systems thinking: connecting people, processes, data, and tools to identify opportunities and build repeatable solutions across the go-to-market motion.

    Strong AI fluency: knowing when to leverage AI and how to build AI-powered workflows or tools that scale product marketing work, with human judgment and quality checks built in.

    Pricing and packaging input for a new tier or add-on (nice to have).

    7+ years in B2B SaaS product marketing, including at least 2 years supporting a sales team selling to mid-market and/or larger accounts.

    Added a sales-led motion on top of a product-led one at a high-growth company, and can show what changed before and after with clear metrics.

    Built a deal toolkit and enablement program from little or nothing, and tied it to a sales metric like win rate or deal size.

    Ran a win/loss or customer research program that changed how a team sold or built.

    Ran an expansion or account-based program for an existing customer base (nice to have).

    Worked in email, martech, or the creator economy.

    You lead without a formal title. You align sales, product, RevOps, and finance on goals, trade-offs, and what success looks like, then keep things moving.

    You advocate for creators in decisions, and you protect the self-serve experience instead of pushing every account toward sales.

    You act with urgency and stay focused on hitting OKRs and owning outcomes.

    Sources indicate that you work in public. You share findings, drafts, and the reasoning behind decisions so others can build on them.

    You connect data to decisions, and you help others get sharper about using it.

    You raise the bar on quality and iterate toward it, and you shape how your team uses AI, from call analysis to keeping battlecards current.

    Experience in only self-serve or only enterprise sales. This role lives in the space between them, and you'll need to understand both.

    Treating enablement as a deck handoff. The work includes coaching reps, measuring what gets used, and revising what doesn't land.

    It has been revealed that wanting a sales playbook already in place. Much of this motion doesn't exist yet, and you'll be building it as you learn.

    Preferring to be measured on output rather than outcomes. You'll share accountability with Sales for win rate, deal size, and expansion revenue.

    Needing extensive approval before acting. You'll be trusted to make calls on speed versus quality and to explain your reasoning.

    Discomfort with direct, candid feedback, especially from sellers on what's working in live deals.

    We're 100% remote with team members across the globe. We work mostly on East Coast time—so if you're based on the West Coast of the United States, Europe, or Asia, you might have a few early mornings or late evenings. We do our best to keep things reasonable, but a little time zone juggling comes with the territory.

    In a recent development, kit has standardized salaries based on position, no matter where you live. For this role, we’re hiring at our level 4 ($166,000). Level is determined based on experience and our interview process.

    We cover up to $2,280 per month toward medical premiums, with dental and vision premiums fully covered. We offer Health Insurance plans through Aetna.

    According to recent reports, $2,000 equipment allowance for your first two years, $1,000 budget every following two years. Manufacturer-provided laptops are issued to every Kit team member and are not included in the equipment budget.

    Individual learning + development budget ($3,500/year).

    Creator meetup budget ($50/month) to connect with creators over coffee, lunch, or other in-person meetups.

    Childcare benefit up to $3,000 annually through JOON.

    Twenty (20) days of paid time off during each year of employment.

    Paid paid vacation: An after-tax bonus of $1,000 for taking five consecutive days of vacation where you’re fully unplugged from work.

    Two weeks of paid sick time each year, including mental health + well being days.

    Twelve (12) weeks paid parental leave and flexible scheduling in your child’s first year.

    Up to six weeks of paid bereavement leave, medical leave, and disaster after six months of employment, two weeks of each paid leave in your first six months.

    Winter Break Closure: Kit closes for a week at the end of December, giving everyone a collective break to enjoy the holiday season. Essential support services remain available, with teams coordinating to ensure coverage during this period.

    Four-week, paid sabbatical after five years with the team.

    Fantastic in-person or virtual retreats with the team twice a year.

    We usually receive a large number of applications, and our goal is to follow up with you within two weeks. You’ll hear from us either way. Here’s what you can expect from the rest of our hiring process:.

    A phone screen with our recruiter (30 min).

    Hiring manager interview (45 min).

    Recent findings suggest that we’ll keep you informed through every step. To get started, complete this application, including a cover letter and answers to the questions on the next page. We read every single application, and your cover letter and responses help put your experience into context.

    Kit is an equal opportunity employer.

    We value diversity in all of its forms. Research tells us that applicants who are female or non-binary, as well as applicants who are people of color, are less likely to apply for roles they do not feel 100% qualified for. If you think you meet more than 50% of our requirements but fewer than 100% of them, please apply.

    We’re imperfect communicators, so think of our job postings as the starting point for discussion rather than proof that you shouldn’t apply.

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Digiday ↗ Open Full Page

    Mail Metro Media’s next creator play is representing them

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1313 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that join us Dec.
    • In a recent development, mail Metro Media now thinks “more like a talent agency” and commissions “like a broadcaster”, according to Hannah Blake, its managing director of creator and newly introduced media.
    • Recent findings suggest that audiences tune in for them, brands pay to reach those audiences, and the deals have grown from around £5,000 apiece to worth seven figures in October.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    In a recent development, mail Metro Media now thinks “more like a talent agency” and commissions “like a broadcaster”, according to Hannah Blake, its managing director of creator and newly introduced media. Its creators have, in other words, become the business.

    Recent findings suggest that audiences tune in for them, brands pay to reach those audiences, and the deals have grown from around £5,000 apiece to worth seven figures in October. Holding on to those creators is now as key as finding them since any one who leaves for an outside agent can take the audience and advertisers along too.

    Blake spelled out that risk on stage at the Digiday Media Strategies London event in October.

    “The huge risk is that we make these people super famous and then they go and get signed by a different agent,” she said.

    It has been revealed that so in September the ad sales arm for the Daily Mail hired David White from Whalar as head of creators, with a brief to build an in-house talent agency that represents its creators and signs outside talent too. White was the first hire for the company’s Stars business in Newly introduced York, the talent management arm that handles creators’ careers beyond brand deals and was also a senior talent manager there.

    What the business ultimately ends up with is still open. Blake described something that “potentially could look more like a talent agency and an employer,” and she hopes to have it in market by the end of the year. The final shape matters because running a talent agency would be a substantial change of job for a newspaper group’s ad sales team. It exists to sell audiences to brands while an agent’s job is to get the best deal for the talent. Mail Metro Media would be trying to do both at once.

    According to recent reports, that’s the potted history of how Mail Metro Media reached this point. The full story is a lot more nuanced.

    Recent findings suggest that it started four years ago when Daily Mail rolled out Eliza, a social-only brand for young women fronted by six fashion and beauty creators. Its hit format, “Guess Which Outfit’s Most Expensive”, puts two women on the street, one in a £10,000 outfit and the other in a high-street copy, and leaves viewers to guess which is which. It kept going viral, people kept coming back and advertisers soon followed. That’s despite it being relatively small next to the rest of the Mail’s portfolio, and yet “we were doing lots of direct advertisers relationships quite quickly”, Blake said. Fast forward to now,  and brands often book content on Eliza and then want its creators posting on their own accounts too, which Mail Metro Media packages into the deal.

    In a recent development, the Mail’s own TikTok was a different story. The Mail and Metro introduced on the platform around the same time as Eliza and the former became the biggest news publisher there, with 20 million followers, on the back of rapid-fire news clips. But the money didn’t follow. “The huge issue was there was no monetization there,” Blake remarked, even though publishers had widely expected TikTok to start paying them for views. Advertisers weren’t keen either, Every rival was posting the same kind of clips and the Daily Mail couldn’t build a brand into footage it had brought in from elsewhere.

    Together, they showed the publisher that the money was in reveals it owned and creators audiences came back for. It shifted course accordingly, and over the past year it relaunched the Mail and Metro on social around repeatable shows it owns, such as the sports debate show “Dugout Debate” with creators at the front and helping shape them. Blake remarked the operation now pulls 5 billion monthly video views across 10 brands and signed its first seven-figure deal last month. With that success comes a new kind of risk. The creators fronting those shows have built followings of their own and “now some of the superstars are beginning to emerge,” Blake said. Left unchecked, the publisher ends up making stars for outside agencies to sign.

    In some ways, the publisher has already been acting like an agent of sorts. Alongside its core bundle where brands pay one flat rate for a run of content with “no differentiation between the talent,” Blake noted it has spent the past year selling individual creators on their own channels. It calls this add-on “Creator Amp.” One example is Mimi Yates, a young journalist who fronts much of the news output and has built a following of her own. Brands can book her as part of a wider campaign or on her own, and on their personal accounts the creators “all set their own rates,” Blake said.

    That arrangement was easy to manage while the talent was still unknown.

    According to recent reports, “When we started, our creators were all emerging,” Blake noted. With bigger names now coming through, the publisher wants something sturdier. “We are now at the point where we’re beginning to formalize that relationship a bit more,” she said, and hiring White was the first step.

    Recent findings suggest that he will recruit from two places. One is from its own staff. The other is outside talent Blake described as “the next generation of emerging news and entertainment talent”.

    Sources indicate that moves like this bring some awkward conversations with them. Daily Mail’s creators are salaried and Nathan Aspell, director of the New Media division, remarked the firm owns the IP they develop. Blake described those same creators setting their own rates on their own channels. How the money is split between the employer and agent will go a long way to deciding whether a breakout star sticks around.

    Axel Springer’s version hands journalists a share of the financial results in return for production, marketing and distribution. Daily Mail hasn’t mentioned what its agency will charge.

    Then there’s the small matter of journalism. The same person can read the headlines and sell the mascara, and the publisher would be both their employer and their agent. That’s a lot of hats for one newsroom.

    White’s first signings will show how far the publisher prepares to take this venture. Blake thinks publishers are headed this way regardless. “I actually think it’s just a byproduct of where the opportunity is,” she noted.

    For a lot of publishers, signing talent still feels like someone else’s business and talk of newsrooms turning into agencies tends to raise eyebrows. Blake sees it as following the money, which increasingly sits with “people-centric IP that exists across multiple different touchpoints”.

    In a recent development, plenty of rivals are following it too. Axel Springer introduced its own spin on the same idea last month, while Hearst did so earlier this week. Increasingly, publishers see a talent operation as the next step in their latest pivot to video, which runs on personalities whose audiences, and the ad money chasing them, follow them wherever they go.

    “Publishers are responding to the audience’s desire for personality-led formats while limiting strategic dependence on individual journalists and managing talent,” mentioned Laura Darcey, research analyst at Enders Analysis.

    Recent findings suggest that editor’s note: An earlier version of this article said David White ran Whalar’s Stars business in Upcoming York. He was the first hire for the division in New York.

    Breaking: Last of the old school buyers, Publicis Media vet John Muszynski prepares to retire

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (834 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that join us Dec.
    • He’s equally comfortable at the negotiating table or on skates in an ice rink.
    • He doesn’t do it himself but he knows principal media is part of the business.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    He’s equally comfortable at the negotiating table or on skates in an ice rink.

    He doesn’t do it himself but he knows principal media is part of the business.

    He’s noted to have once humbled the CEO of a major cable network group by holding back $200 million of his clients’ media spend when that CEO tried to bully him into significant price increases.

    According to recent reports, he’s the longest-serving head of investment in media. And now, John Muszynski, legendary media investment executive with Publicis Media, plans to retire.

    After 45 years at one holding firm and negotiating nearly as many upfronts over that span, the chairman of Publicis Media Exchange (PMX) U.S., is stepping down from a full-time role this year, although he looks to continue to consult with the holdco.

    Chicago-based Muszynski, who oversees decision-making on what Publicis estimates to be 40% of the U.S. video marketplace inventory, is arguably the last of the old-school heads of investment that have seen the upfronts morph into the byzantine bazaar it is today.

    “For nearly five decades, I’ve had a front row seat to the industry’s transformation,” Muszynski told Digiday. “It’s gone from three networks to always-on content spanning the entire digital ecosystem. It’s been fascinating to be a part of it all.”.

    It has been revealed that the avid ice hockey fan, hunter and fisherman (when he’s not negotiating) got his start in 1981 as a planner for Leo Burnett’s burgeoning media unit, handling longtime Publicis clients including Kimberly-Clark, McDonald’s and Kellogg’s. That unit eventually became standalone media agency Starcom, for which he rose to CEO of Starcom USA from 2005-2009. He then helped to build Spark Foundry from a 65-person boutique into a 3,000-person media agency.

    In 2016, Publicis formed Publicis Media Exchange, which harnessed the collective buying clout of what was then Starcom, Mediavest, Spark, Zenith, Optimedia and Blue 449 media agencies. He was the lead negotiator when that formed, and became chairman of the group in 2022.

    The execs who sat across from him at the negotiating table stated they always felt they got a fair shake — in part because Muszynski always came prepared, was knowledgable and true to his word.

    Sources indicate that “John has been a tremendous influence on generations of marketers, agency team members and publishers,” remarked Mark Marshall, chairman of global advertising and partnerships at NBCUniversal. “He has always put his clients’ objectives at the forefront and pushed all of us to deliver for those clients. He is the epitome of ‘a handshake is his word’.”.

    Sources indicate that rita Ferro, president, global advertising, disney, was even more personal in her assessment of working with Muszynski. “John is a legend in this business and from the moment we met, he became a trusted partner and more importantly a dear friend,” she remarked.

    Sean Moran, COO at Evergreen Trading agency, who negotiated with Muszynski during his 24 years as an ad sales exec with Viacom until 2020, thinks of Muszynski as a contemporary of the old-school buyers of the TV business, from Grey Advertising’s Jon Mandel to UM’s Donna Wolfe, and from Omnicom’s John Swift to GroupM’s Rino Scanzoni.

    “When I was running MTV and we had a substantial upfront event, and had to get people there, if I could get John Muszynski to fly in and come to my event, that was a huge win,” mentioned Moran. ”He represented so much gravitas. Obviously he controlled a lot of budgets, but it was also because he was so smart and yet had such empathy for good people. You couldn’t bullshit him. He was a good Midwestern guy who could talk about a great deal over over a steak, but he did his homework and knew his numbers.”.

    It has been revealed that moran said Muszynski often set the marketplace as “the main controller” of the upfronts. “One of his negotiating tactics was, ‘Yeah, I haven’t seen everything, but boy, it looks down’,” said Moran. “If he respected your inventory, you could do a deal with him fairly promptly and cut through the chaff. He was known to pull that with one or two people that were at the front of the line, and protect his clients. He would therefore set the marketplace for himself. It was very smart.”.

    Recent findings suggest that although Muszynski will retire from his full-time position at PMX, he will stay on to consult through 2027, working with Joel Lunenfeld who leads PMX globally and Mark Griffin, who oversees all investment in the U.S. as chief investment officer.

    Senior Product Marketing Manager - Upmarket at Kit

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1733 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realworkfromanywhere

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Kit is the email marketing platform experts choose to grow their audience, deepen their relationships, and build a business around the work they love.
    • Kit's most established creators run real companies, with teams, large lists, dedicated sending needs, and a buying process that our self-serve motion wasn't built to serve.
    • You'll define who this buyer is, write the story that resonates and wins with them, and build the GTM strategy to drive inbound pipeline for our sales team.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Kit is the email marketing platform experts choose to grow their audience, deepen their relationships, and build a business around the work they love. For coaches, YouTubers, authors, podcasters, and other creatives, there isn't a better marketing hub to rely on to grow audiences, automate email marketing, and sell digital products — all within one platform.More importantly, there isn't a team more committed to helping creators earn a living. We're on a mission to help creators earn $1 billion using our creator marketing platform. We have always been 100% independent and 100% remote.We are proud to have built a product that our customers love, and we look for people who have enthusiasm and belief in our mission, vision, and values to join our team. We're also embracing AI thoughtfully — both in how we build and how we hire to ensure our team is adaptable, innovative, and ready for what's next.

    Kit's most established creators run real companies, with teams, large lists, dedicated sending needs, and a buying process that our self-serve motion wasn't built to serve. Because this part of our business is growing, we're looking for a Senior Product Marketing Manager, Scaling Creators to own how Kit wins, lands, and expands these businesses through a sales-assisted motion that sits alongside our self-serve product.

    You'll define who this buyer is, write the story that resonates and wins with them, and build the GTM strategy to drive inbound pipeline for our sales team. When these creators choose Kit and grow on it, they build more valuable businesses, and that's the outcome this role exists for.

    This is a full-time individual contributor role ideal for someone who has added an upmarket sales-led motion to a product-led company before and wants their work measured in win rate and deal size.

    You'll report to Christina Lhi, Head of Marketing, and work alongside two other experienced Product Marketing Managers on Kit's product marketing team. Together, you'll keep the self-serve and sales-assisted stories feeling like one Kit.

    You'll spend a lot of your time with:.

    Our sales leadership, on who we sell to, the deal toolkit, enablement, and win/loss.

    Account Executives and Solutions Consultants, on demo narratives, discovery, and technical and migration proof.

    Product, on packaging, launches, and roadmap input.

    RevOps and analytics, on how accounts get routed to sales, attribution, and pricing decisions.

    Creator Success, on case studies, customer references, and expansion plays.

    Demand gen, content, and events, on campaigns and events for established creators.

    In a recent development, first Week: Dive into our onboarding curriculum in Notion and learn Kit's product, pricing, and current positioning. Attend Get-To-Know-You (GTKY) meetings with marketing, sales, Solutions Consultants, RevOps, and Creator Success. Get access to our CRM, call recordings, and product analytics, and start listening to recent sales calls. Understand how product marketing at the moment works at Kit.

    Industry observers note that first Month: Shadow 15+ sales calls and talk with 10 established creators, including recent wins, losses, and churned accounts. Audit the sales content reps use today and how product usage currently routes accounts to sales. Set baselines with RevOps for win rate, sales cycle, deal size, and expansion revenue. Share a written point of view with the entire growth team on who our established creator buyer is and the three biggest gaps in how we sell to them. And an action strategy on how we can win these creators.

    First Year: Sales runs on messaging and tools you built, pitch with confidence and we drive 2X inbound MQLs from when you started. You’ll own and lead our channel strategy, setting the vision, driving cross-functional alignment, and partnering with Marketing to bring it to life. You'll run a quarterly win/loss program and share what you learn openly, build a clear path for sales leads on our website, and make sure rolls out that matter to larger accounts ship with both a self-serve and a sales-assisted version. Your work has a direct impact on helping Kit reach $100,000,000 ARR while protecting the self-serve engine that got us here.

    Segmentation and buyer definition: turning firmographic and product usage data into a clear picture of who to sell to and when.

    Messaging and positioning for a sales-assisted buyer, including competitive differentiation and objection handling.

    Sales enablement that reps actually use: demo narratives, discovery guides, business cases, and battlecards.

    Writing and storytelling that turns product depth into a business case a non-technical buyer can act on.

    Working with CRM, product analytics, and pipeline data to measure funnel conversion, win rate, and deal size.

    Customer and market/competitor research, including win/loss interviews and call analysis.

    Systems thinking: connecting people, processes, data, and tools to identify opportunities and build repeatable solutions across the go-to-market motion.

    Strong AI fluency: knowing when to leverage AI and how to build AI-powered workflows or tools that scale product marketing work, with human judgment and quality checks built in.

    Pricing and packaging input for a newly introduced tier or add-on (nice to have).

    7+ years in B2B SaaS product marketing, including at least 2 years supporting a sales team selling to mid-market and/or larger accounts.

    Added a sales-led motion on top of a product-led one at a high-growth manufacturer, and can show what changed before and after with clear metrics.

    Built a deal toolkit and enablement program from little or nothing, and tied it to a sales metric like win rate or deal size.

    Ran a win/loss or customer research program that changed how a team sold or built.

    Ran an expansion or account-based program for an existing customer base (nice to have).

    Worked in email, martech, or the creator economy.

    You lead without a formal title. You align sales, product, RevOps, and finance on goals, trade-offs, and what success looks like, then keep things moving.

    You advocate for creators in decisions, and you protect the self-serve experience instead of pushing every account toward sales.

    You act with urgency and stay focused on hitting OKRs and owning outcomes.

    You work in public. You share findings, drafts, and the reasoning behind decisions so others can build on them.

    You connect data to decisions, and you help others get sharper about using it.

    You raise the bar on quality and iterate toward it, and you shape how your team uses AI, from call analysis to keeping battlecards current.

    In a recent development, experience in only self-serve or only enterprise sales. This role lives in the space between them, and you'll need to understand both.

    Recent findings suggest that treating enablement as a deck handoff. The work includes coaching reps, measuring what gets used, and revising what doesn't land.

    Wanting a sales playbook already in place. Much of this motion doesn't exist yet, and you'll be building it as you learn.

    Preferring to be measured on output rather than outcomes. You'll share accountability with Sales for win rate, deal size, and expansion revenue.

    Needing extensive approval before acting. You'll be trusted to make calls on speed versus quality and to explain your reasoning.

    Discomfort with direct, candid feedback, especially from sellers on what's working in live deals.

    According to recent reports, we're 100% remote with team members across the globe. We work mostly on East Coast time—so if you're based on the West Coast of the United States, Europe, or Asia, you might have a few early mornings or late evenings. We do our best to keep things reasonable, but a little time zone juggling comes with the territory.

    Kit has standardized salaries based on position, no matter where you live. For this role, we’re hiring at our level 4 ($166,000). Level is determined based on experience and our interview process.

    We cover up to $2,280 per month toward medical premiums, with dental and vision premiums fully covered. We offer Health Insurance prepares through Aetna.

    $2,000 equipment allowance for your first two years, $1,000 budget every following two years. Tech giant-provided laptops are issued to every Kit team member and are not included in the equipment budget.

    Individual learning + development budget ($3,500/year).

    Creator meetup budget ($50/month) to connect with creators over coffee, lunch, or other in-person meetups.

    Childcare benefit up to $3,000 annually through JOON.

    Twenty (20) days of paid time off during each year of employment.

    Paid paid vacation: An after-tax bonus of $1,000 for taking five consecutive days of vacation where you’re fully unplugged from work.

    Two weeks of paid sick time each year, including mental health + well being days.

    Twelve (12) weeks paid parental leave and flexible scheduling in your child’s first year.

    Up to six weeks of paid bereavement leave, medical leave, and disaster after six months of employment, two weeks of each paid leave in your first six months.

    According to recent reports, winter Break Closure: Kit closes for a week at the end of December, giving everyone a collective break to enjoy the holiday season. Essential support services remain available, with teams coordinating to ensure coverage during this period.

    Four-week, paid sabbatical after five years with the team.

    Fantastic in-person or virtual retreats with the team twice a year.

    We usually receive a large number of applications, and our goal is to follow up with you within two weeks. You’ll hear from us either way. Here’s what you can expect from the rest of our hiring process:.

    A phone screen with our recruiter (30 min).

    Hiring manager interview (45 min).

    We’ll keep you informed through every step. To get started, complete this application, including a cover letter and answers to the questions on the next page. We read every single application, and your cover letter and responses help put your experience into context.

    Kit is an equal opportunity employer.

    We value diversity in all of its forms. Research tells us that applicants who are female or non-binary, as well as applicants who are people of color, are less likely to apply for roles they do not feel 100% qualified for. If you think you meet more than 50% of our requirements but fewer than 100% of them, please apply.

    We’re imperfect communicators, so think of our job postings as the starting point for discussion rather than proof that you shouldn’t apply.

    Kit does not discriminate on the basis of race, sex, color, religion, age, national origin, marital status, disability, veteran status, genetic information, sexual orientation, gender identity or any other reason prohibited by law in provision of employment opportunities and benefits.

    #101464. Correcting the TV ad market’s imperfect shift to streaming

    Correcting the TV ad market’s imperfect shift to streaming

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (681 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.
    • Evan Rutchik, president and Chief Strategy Officer, Viamedia.ai.
    • The TV ad industry’s shift from linear to streaming is real, but the financial truth underlying that shift may not align with many people’s perception of the transition.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    Evan Rutchik, president and Chief Strategy Officer, Viamedia.ai.

    The TV ad industry’s shift from linear to streaming is real, but the financial truth underlying that shift may not align with many people’s perception of the transition. That’s because the movement of ad budgets from linear to streaming has hardly been evenly paced.

    Streaming’s share of ad revenue is indeed growing at major media companies, including The Walt Disney Organization, Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery. But their earnings tell a different story: Linear revenue is falling faster than streaming revenue is rising. The shift is happening, but it’s not benefiting content owners as expected.

    The core problem is a supply-demand imbalance. Streaming ad revenue is growing through increased volume, not higher prices. Upcoming inventory floods in, making cheap inventory abundant. As major subscription services continue to promote free ad-supported streaming tiers, the buyers’ market will only continue.

    The solution is to grow demand, not increase prices. Fortunately, the ad dollars needed to support the streaming market already exist, sitting in local and midmarket budgets that haven’t been able to buy national CTV efficiently. The opportunity is to bring these advertisers into the broader video and streaming market, then develop ways to keep them investing.

    Correcting the imbalance requires creating new demand, then ensuring that content quality and product performance are strong enough to eventually shift pricing dynamics.

    In a recent development, when it comes to growth, the glut of cheap national SVOD supply may be a problem for programmers, but it’s an opportunity for local and midmarket advertisers. If the current streaming market is largely aimed at Fortune 500 companies, the industry has to consider the thousands of smaller advertisers that make steady annual investments in local linear buys. Taken collectively, these advertisers represent billions of dollars in ad budgets.

    Because these advertisers have smaller budgets, many haven’t tried streaming. It is more cost-efficient for them to execute local and spot buys on linear than to invest in targeted or national streaming campaigns. These advertisers are still seeing real success reaching millions of linear viewers, so they understand the power of TV. They just need an entry point for CTV. Solving this issue would allow demand to flow steadily into the market.

    Sources indicate that once that demand enters the market, additional steps must happen. CPMs fall when inventory is sold as undifferentiated tonnage. With platforms like Disney+ and Netflix exploring free ad-supported tiers, even more low-cost supply will enter the market. But cheap supply that doesn’t perform isn’t worth an advertiser’s investment. If that inventory doesn’t deliver results for advertisers outside the Fortune 500, those advertisers will invest their budgets elsewhere, creating another demand imbalance.

    It has been revealed that the answer lies in household addressability. While this is available on some streaming platforms, it’s still largely absent from the overall TV market, including linear. Household-level addressability turns cheap impressions into targeted impressions worth buying, even within highly premium inventory. The more information brands have about who will see their ads and whether those ads are likely to resonate with the viewer, the more they are likely to pay.

    Recent findings suggest that it is no secret that streaming is the future of TV, and shifting revenue numbers reflect that. To build a sustainable future for media companies and advertisers, the entire ecosystem must first provide ease of access and then addressability.

    Making streaming easier to buy at scale would help solve the demand problem. Once more advertisers are in the market, addressability creates greater competition for impressions, solving the pricing imbalance.

    This future is out there, provided the industry takes a few steps in the right direction.

    Partner insights from Viamedia.ai.

    Holiday marketing is changing: CTV/streaming and TV ads are gaining traction in 2026.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that join us Dec.
    • OpenAI has revised the terms for its new ChatGPT Business Hub days after its launch.
    • In a recent development, released last week, the Business Hub gives businesses that verify their accounts direct data on how their websites appear in ChatGPT, including mentions, profile views, clicks and discovery topics.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    OpenAI has revised the terms for its new ChatGPT Business Hub days after its launch. The change came after Digiday reported that lawyers viewed the original language as potentially limiting businesses’ ability to bring certain legal claims against the company.

    In a recent development, released last week, the Business Hub gives businesses that verify their accounts direct data on how their websites appear in ChatGPT, including mentions, profile views, clicks and discovery topics. For publishers, it’s a first-party view of activity they’ve largely had to estimate.

    Industry observers note that before the revision, Section 10 of OpenAI’s terms of service for businesses using ChatGPT appeared to require those businesses to give up certain legal claims against OpenAI, lawyers told Digiday. They mentioned the language could apply to claims involving content published on their websites, before they signed up.

    Alan Chapell, privacy expert and founder of Chapell and Associates, remarked publishers who signed up for ChatGPT’s Business Hub and accepted the terms could have faced restrictions on how they pursued such claims against OpenAI.

    It has been revealed that the terms included a mandatory arbitration provision and class-action waiver, potentially requiring businesses to resolve disputes individually and outside of court, Chapell mentioned. The provision was broadly worded to cover certain claims that arose before the agreement was accepted, he explained.

    Businesses had 30 days to opt out of arbitration, but if they did not, they could have faced limits on their ability to obtain evidence, pursue appeals and establish legal precedent through public court proceedings, Chapell added.

    Hours after Digiday first contacted OpenAI on Nov. 18, the terms were revised. They now include a waiver of businesses’ rights to seek a court order preventing OpenAI from using certain customer data, according to an IP and tech lawyer, who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

    In a recent development, “There are still some restrictions here but they don’t leave a customer completely without recourse. A customer could still, even if not entirely practical, sue for monetary damages,” they remarked.

    When approached for comment, an OpenAI spokesperson said the previous version of the terms “were not intended to cover this scenario,” and confirmed it updated the terms on Nov. 18.

    “We continually evaluate the language in our Terms to make sure they are as clear as possible,” the spokesperson added in a statement. “The updated terms replace the separate ‘covered claims’ provision with language in Section 5.2 that ties the release to claims arising from a business’s Business Agent, including the use of customer data with that agent.”.

    According to recent reports, one industry exec, who requested anonymity, told Digiday they advised publishers’ legal teams to be cautious around some of the potential implications of OpenAI’s terms for businesses, after they were originally published on Nov. 10.

    Although the terms have been revised, several lawyers who spoke to Digiday noted the original version was likely deliberate.

    Recent findings suggest that “This is certainly not an oversight because they put these terms out there,” remarked Gary Kibel, partner at law firm Davis+ Gilbert, which advises media and advertising clients. “It was incredibly intentional, and they were seeking to use this opportunity to get a release and wavier for any of these claims. It seems to be quite aggressive to do that.”.

    Kibel noted the revised terms still require businesses to waive certain legal claims related to their use of ChatGPT Business Hub and its AI Business Agents (essentially a business-specific chatbot), but no longer extend that waiver to unrelated legal disputes with OpenAI.

    Industry observers note that openAI’s changes come just weeks after Meta faced major backlash from publishers over its new commercial terms, which would have allowed the manufacturer to scrape the websites of Meta Business account people. The proposed changes spurred a global, coordinated pushback from publishers, trade bodies, and government officials and regulators. In response, Meta declared it would pause the rollout until it has had time to explain the changes to key stakeholders and partners.

    According to recent reports, openAI’s terms revision also follows tensions between publishers and AI companies over the use of published content. Documents unsealed in The Upcoming York Times’ lawsuit against OpenAI and Microsoft two months ago revealed tech giants were treating published content as free fuel for AI products that threatened their very existence.

    Whatever prompted the revision, it may do little to ease publishers’ broader concerns about how AI companies use their content, and the terms attached to upcoming tools built around that content.

    Grand Theft Auto 6 has its own content creator cottage industry, with millions of views and a crowded, competitive marketplace.

    ChatGPT’s new AI visibility and click data can help inform publishers’ GEO strategies and complement third-party analytics.

    Creators are tapping into their massive content libraries for syndication opportunities that pay dividends.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The digital media publisher BuzzFeed has hired Chris Poydenis, the co-founder and longtime chief revenue officer of the influencer marketing manufacturer Influential, as its new chief revenue officer, the company announced Monday.
    • Poydenis spent more than 10 years building Influential, which he and his partners sold to Publicis in 2024 for $500 million, according to the organization.
    • Poydenis is also bringing along Jesse Batres, most recently the executive vice president and head of national sales and partnerships at Influential, to BuzzFeed, where he will serve as its newly introduced president of sales and partnerships.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The digital media publisher BuzzFeed has hired Chris Poydenis, the co-founder and longtime chief revenue officer of the influencer marketing manufacturer Influential, as its new chief revenue officer, the company announced Monday.

    Poydenis spent more than 10 years building Influential, which he and his partners sold to Publicis in 2024 for $500 million, according to the organization.

    Poydenis is also bringing along Jesse Batres, most recently the executive vice president and head of national sales and partnerships at Influential, to BuzzFeed, where he will serve as its newly introduced president of sales and partnerships. Both executives start Monday.

    “I had breakfast with [CEO Byron Allen], and it didn’t take more than 30 minutes for me to be completely aligned and bought in,” Poydenis noted. “BuzzFeed already has such beloved brands—with Tasty and HuffPost. There’s an incredible base to build from.”.

    The hires come at a precarious moment for BuzzFeed. Six months after Allen took a controlling stake in the firm, the publisher has cut more than a third of its staff, and its stock has cratered, all while it tries to reinvent itself as a video-first, free-streaming platform.

    Whether that pivot works will depend largely on whether advertisers follow BuzzFeed into the living room, a job that will now fall to Poydenis and Batres.

    Under its new ownership, BuzzFeed aims to pair content from its existing brands with premium content from Allen Media Group and distribute it across a connected television app, the website, and the mobile app, according to Poydenis.

    The publisher also prepares to expand into user-generated and creator content, according to The Newly introduced York Times.

    In a recent development, “If you look at what other streaming platforms are doing, they are all clamoring to figure out a way to infuse the creator economy into their product,” Poydenis said. “With [Batres] and I coming over, we’re in lockstep with [Allen] to make that a reality.”.

    FOR Scoops, Sharp Analysis, and Insider Context.

    In a recent development, the goal is to recruit more creators and build a platform where they can upload their libraries and monetize them with brands. In doing so, the creators would be adding to BuzzFeed’s 75 million monthly active customers and 2 billion monthly content views, according to Poydenis.

    Still, the odds facing the firm are long.

    Allen took over as chairman and CEO in May, after his holding company, Allen Family Digital, agreed to pay $120 million for a 52% stake: $20 million at closing and the remaining $100 million over five years. In tandem with the deal, cofounder Jonah Peretti stepped down as CEO to become its fresh president of AI.

    Before the deal, BuzzFeed had warned investors that it was at risk of not continuing as a business, citing $58.4 million in debt and millions in annual losses, according to The Latest York Times.

    It has been revealed that in July, the company laid off about 180 employees across BuzzFeed, HuffPost, and Tasty, roughly 35% of its workforce, according to an SEC filing. Earlier this month, its stock fell 38% in a single morning after a disappointing third-quarter earnings report, sinking to $0.57 per share, according to Futurism.

    For Poydenis, the turnaround is part of the appeal.

    Industry observers note that “At my heart, I’m a competitor, and I’m a builder,” Poydenis mentioned. “After the acquisition with Publicis, I feel like for me the job was done. [Allen] is offering me an opportunity to go in somewhere with a phenomenal foundation and to build once again.”.

    Mark Stenberg is ADWEEK's senior media reporter.

    Tech Report: Why more brands are paying creators to make their ads

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1012 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that join us Dec.
    • This article is part of an ongoing series detailing the most notable information readers need to know about the ad industry’s most complex topics.
    • Industry observers note that brands paying influencers to make campaign creative have become key drivers of investment in the booming creator economy.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    This article is part of an ongoing series detailing the most notable information readers need to know about the ad industry’s most complex topics. More from the series →.

    Industry observers note that brands paying influencers to make campaign creative have become key drivers of investment in the booming creator economy. Creative agencies might want to take note.

    It has been revealed that “You get the authentic, scroll-stopping content that people want to engage each with. But you also get the reach,” mentioned Katy Ball, head of social at M&C Saatchi Sport & Entertainment.

    As spending on paid social channels — and video in particular — continues to rise, demand for creative assets to appear in those ad slots is increasing.

    The number of assets attached to individual campaigns has risen 30% in the last five years, according to a CreativeX study of 115,990 ad campaigns, representing $11 billion in ad spend. Per the study, just five assets receive 88% of media investment in an average campaign.

    The need for more campaign assets is fueling the growth of asset-led spending, the fastest growing segment of the creator economy, according to a report published this week by research consultancy Madison & Wall.

    Currently, 12% of the $112 billion spent on creators globally goes towards creators producing ads on behalf of brands, per the study. That’s expected to rise 16% every year through 2030.

    The days when brands principally paid creators to rent their following are rapidly disappearing. Influencers are now media partners, ambassadors and increasingly, cogs in the creative production supply chain. And brands see creator-made ads as a solution to their social asset shortage.

    Industry observers note that “For us, the appeal is simple. Buying space in someone’s feed doesn’t mean you’ve earned their attention. Good creators understand what their audiences care about and how to give them something worth stopping for,” remarked Jared Kozel, co-founder and chief creative officer at agency Super Nice. “That’s valuable creative judgment to bring into an ad no matter the brand or category.”.

    Influencer marketing experts note that several different but related practices are included under the broader umbrella of creator-led production.

    While some brands simply pay creators a fee in order to receive video or still assets for use in a campaign, whitelisting (also called “dark advertising”) has become a favored method of managing such arrangements.

    In this context, an influencer grants a brand limited access to their social media accounts, allowing them to book a paid media campaign through that account, using assets made by the creator while taking advantage of discrete audience targeting.

    “What we’re seeing is a lot of recutting of media spend to be allocated towards creator development in order to fund whitelisting,” mentioned Olivia Wedderburn, head of influence at Born Social.

    Madison & Wall’s research suggested that funding for creative production may also be coming from PR, social or experimental budgets, as well as traditional media or production pots of money.

    Another related practice, user generated content, sees brands paying regular social media users to license their content as creative assets in ad campaigns.

    “They have to feed their their content engines, and they’re opening up as many different avenues as they can,” said Andy Ryan, co-founder at social and influencer agency Komodo.

    The relative low cost of working with influencers, versus creative production agencies, is the primary driver behind brand spending on creator-made assets.

    Although production spending is often a small fraction of an overall campaign budget, marketers are keen to squeeze every non-working (that is, non-media) dollar for all it’s worth. While that same desire is pushing some brands toward generative AI production techniques, others are turning to creators.

    Sources indicate that but as this type of spending grows, so to does the need to manage it effectively. “It’s never been more complicated to negotiate usage rights or exclusivity,” said Wedderburn.

    Billion Dollar Boy, for example, recently added features to its Companion creator management tool designed to better facilitate creator-led production efforts and manage usage rights negotiations.

    “The creator economy has never been more competitive, heightening the urgency for brands to understand the market context,” stated Thomas Walters, the agency’s chief innocation officer and co-founder.

    Recent findings suggest that at the same time, increased brand spending in this area is already leading to an uptick in the fees commanded by some creators. Last year, agency practitioners reported creator rates ticking up 10-20% due to demand for expanded rights.

    There’s also some evidence to show that creator-made assets perform as well as, or even better than, traditional advertising spots in a social context.

    A report by System1, WPP Media and Goat published in June found that creator ads achieved 3.2X the brand-awareness lift for category leader ads as traditional advertising creative.

    “We’re seeing a lot of brands say that is more valuable in terms of conversion and reach than some of the quick-and-dirty assets they previously would have relied on,” noted Wedderburn.

    That’s not unexpected. Audiences recognize the visual cues, language and production methods employed by creators as native to TikTok or Instagram, while clocking films shot on a closed set or using more traditional methods as foreign that same environment, a lesson that major advertisers like Nike are reluctantly absorbing.

    Industry observers note that “If programs are set up correctly, creators can deliver volume and variety faster and more cost effectively than a traditional production cycle,” said Nicholas Spiro, chief commercial officer, Viral Nation. “The shift we’re seeing is brands starting to plan creators across their media budgets, rather than as a separate influencer line item alone.”.

    Holiday marketing is changing: CTV/streaming and TV ads are gaining traction in 2026.

    In a recent development, gap Inc. has tapped boy band Just Your Type (JYT) for a multi-year partnership and rolled out “The Agency,” a scripted microseries made for Banana Republic.

    Consulting giants Deloitte Digital and Accenture Song have started selling marketing in the C-suite with a fresh push.

    Anthropic claims no to ads but Wall Street may have other ideas

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (865 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
